title: Concurrency
summary: Share data between tasks without corrupting it: races, locks, atomic operations, semaphores, channels and deadlock.

steps.title: Threads, tasks and races
body: A **thread** is one path of execution. A computer with several cores can run several threads at the very same moment. A **task** is a unit of work; `Task.Run` hands it to a pool of threads, so you rarely create threads yourself.
So far your async code mostly *waited* for things. Now several tasks will be *working* at once, on the same data. That is where the trouble starts.
```csharp
int count = 0;
var a = Task.Run(() => { for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) count++; });
var b = Task.Run(() => { for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) count++; });
await Task.WhenAll(a, b);
Console.WriteLine(count);     // 200000? Often less.
`count++` looks like one step but is three: **read** the value, **add** one, **write** it back. Two threads can both read 41, both add one, and both write 42. One increment is lost.
This is a **race condition**: the result depends on timing. Races are nasty because the code usually works, and fails only now and then.

steps.prompt: Four tasks each run `count++` 1,000 times on the same variable with no protection. What can you say about the final value?
options: It is at most 4000, and may be lower on some runs
The program throws an exception when two tasks collide
steps.explain: Lost updates only ever lose increments, and nothing warns you. The same program can print 4000 a hundred times and 3997 the next.

steps.title: lock: one at a time
body: The cure is to make read-add-write happen as one unbroken unit. A `lock` lets only **one thread at a time** into a block of code. Everyone else waits at the door.
```csharp
object gate = new();
int count = 0;
void Increment()
lock (gate)
count++;
- The object in the parentheses is only a key. Every piece of code that touches `count` must lock on the **same** object.
- Use a private object made just for this purpose.
- Keep the locked block short. While one thread is inside, the others are doing nothing.
- You cannot `await` inside a `lock`. The compiler refuses.

steps.title: Fix the race
prompt: `CountVisits` starts 8 tasks that each record 20,000 visits. It should return exactly **160,000**, but it loses some.
Fix the race. Keep the 8 tasks; the point is to make them share the counter safely.
template: Dojo.Eq("8 tasks x 20,000 visits is exactly 160,000", 160000, await CountVisits());
Dojo.Eq("And exactly 160,000 again on a second run", 160000, await CountVisits());

require.message: Protects the counter with lock or Interlocked

hints: The line `visits++` is a read, an add and a write. Two tasks must never be in the middle of it together.
Create one `object gate = new();` before the loop, outside the tasks, so that all 8 share it.

steps.title: Interlocked, ConcurrentDictionary and Parallel
body: A `lock` is the general tool. For common cases there are sharper ones.
**`Interlocked`** performs one small operation on one number as a single, uninterruptible step. No lock needed:
```csharp
Interlocked.Increment(ref count);
Interlocked.Add(ref total, 25);

**`ConcurrentDictionary`** (in `System.Collections.Concurrent`) is a dictionary that many threads may use at once. An ordinary `Dictionary` can be corrupted by that. Its methods combine check-then-act into one safe step:
```csharp
var votes = new ConcurrentDictionary<string, int>();
votes.AddOrUpdate("tea", 1, (key, old) => old + 1);    // add as 1, or add 1 to what is there
**`Parallel.For`** runs the body of a loop on several threads and returns when all of them are done:
```csharp
Parallel.For(0, 4, i => Interlocked.Add(ref total, i));
> **Tip:** The safest shared data is no shared data. If each task can return its own result and you combine them afterwards, there is nothing to protect.

steps.prompt: The order in which the loop bodies run is unknown. The result is not. What does this program print?
steps.explain: 0, 2 and 4 count as tea; 1, 3 and 5 as coffee. Four additions of 10 make 40. Both tools guarantee that no update is lost, whatever the timing.

steps.title: Deadlock
body: Locks solve races and introduce a new failure: two threads each holding a lock the other one needs. Neither can continue. Neither will ever let go. The program does not crash; it just stops.
```csharp
void Transfer(Account from, Account to, decimal amount)
lock (from)
lock (to)
from.Balance -= amount;
to.Balance += amount;

Thread 1 calls `Transfer(a, b, 10)` and locks `a`. At the same moment thread 2 calls `Transfer(b, a, 5)` and locks `b`. Now thread 1 waits for `b` and thread 2 waits for `a`, forever. That is a **deadlock**.
How to stay out of trouble:
- Hold one lock at a time whenever you can.
- If you must hold two, **always take them in the same order** everywhere in the program.
- Never call unknown code (a callback, an event) while holding a lock.

steps.prompt: Thread 1 calls `Transfer(a, b, 10)` while thread 2 calls `Transfer(b, a, 5)`, and both hang forever. Which change fixes the deadlock?
code: void Transfer(Account from, Account to, decimal amount)
options: Always lock the account with the lower `Id` first, whichever direction the money moves
Swap the two lines inside the inner block
steps.explain: With one agreed order, both threads go for the same account first. One gets it and finishes; the other waits and then finishes. Sleeping makes the deadlock *more* likely, and swapping `from` and `to` just mirrors the same bug.

steps.title: SemaphoreSlim: at most N at once
body: A lock admits one. A **semaphore** admits a fixed number. It is how you say *download these 100 files, but only 4 at a time*.
```csharp
var gate = new SemaphoreSlim(4);     // four free slots
async Task DownloadOne(string url)
await gate.WaitAsync();           // take a slot, waiting if all four are busy
try
await DownloadAsync(url);
finally
gate.Release();               // give the slot back, even after an error
Unlike `lock`, a semaphore may be held across an `await`. That makes `new SemaphoreSlim(1)` the usual stand-in for a lock in async code.
The `try`/`finally` matters. A slot that is never released is gone for good, and after four failures everything waits forever.
For the simple case of *do this for every item, N at a time*, `Parallel.ForEachAsync` with a `MaxDegreeOfParallelism` option does the bookkeeping for you.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines so that a slot is taken before the download and is always given back, even when the download throws.
steps.explain: Wait first, outside the `try`: if waiting fails you hold no slot, so there is nothing to release. Then `finally` guarantees the release.

steps.title: Channels: producers and consumers
body: Often the cleanest design shares no variables at all. One side **produces** work items, the other side **consumes** them, and a thread-safe queue sits in between. That queue is a `Channel<T>`, from `System.Threading.Channels`.
```csharp
using System.Threading.Channels;
var channel = Channel.CreateBounded<int>(10);     // holds at most 10 waiting items
async Task Produce()
for (int i = 1; i <= 100; i++)
await channel.Writer.WriteAsync(i);       // waits while the channel is full
channel.Writer.Complete();                    // no more items are coming
async Task Consume()
await foreach (int item in channel.Reader.ReadAllAsync())
Console.WriteLine(item);
}                                                 // the loop ends once the channel is complete and empty
- A **bounded** channel pushes back: a fast producer is made to wait for slow consumers instead of filling up memory.
- Start several `Consume()` tasks and you have a pool of workers. Each item goes to exactly one of them.
- `Complete()` is how consumers learn they can stop. Forget it and they wait forever.

steps.title: Background autosave
prompt: **Sidekick piece: autosave.** In `sk shell` you change things quickly; saving after every keystroke would hammer the disk. Sidekick hands snapshots to a background saver that only ever writes the **latest** one. Your `Snapshot` and `TaskData` records are given (the tests use them).

- Constructor `Autosaver(Func<T, Task> save)`: create a bounded channel of capacity 1 with `BoundedChannelFullMode.DropOldest`, and start one background worker (`Task.Run`) that reads every item with `await foreach` and awaits `save(item)`.
- `public int Saved { get; }`: how many saves have finished.
- `void Request(T snapshot)`: hand it to the channel without waiting (`TryWrite`). While a save is running, a newer request replaces any older one still waiting.
- `DisposeAsync()`: complete the writer, then await the worker, so the last request is written before it returns.
saver.Request("A");   // the worker starts saving A
saver.Request("B"); saver.Request("C"); saver.Request("D");   // only D waits
starter: public int Saved { get; private set; }
solution: readonly Channel<T> pending = Channel.CreateBounded<T>(new BoundedChannelOptions(1) { FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.DropOldest });
public int Saved { get; private set; }
template: Dojo.Eq("while a save runs, newer requests replace older ones: A then only D", new List<string> { "A", "D" }, dojoSaved);
Dojo.Eq("Saved counts the saves that ran", 2, dojoSaver.Saved);
var snapshot = new Snapshot(new List<TaskData> { new(1, "Fix login", 45, 20, false, "bug", "web", null, null) }, new List<TimeEntry>());
await using (var saver = new Autosaver<Snapshot>(async s => { await Task.Delay(5); written = s; }))
Dojo.Check("DisposeAsync waits until the last snapshot is written", ReferenceEquals(snapshot, written), "the snapshot was not saved before DisposeAsync finished");
Dojo.Eq("disposing with nothing requested is fine", 0, idle.Saved);
enum Status { Todo, Doing, Blocked, Done }
record TimeEntry(int TaskId, DateTime Start, DateTime End)
public static bool CanMove(Status from, Status to) => (from, to) switch
(Status.Doing, Status.Todo or Status.Blocked or Status.Done) => true,
record TaskData(int Id, string Title, int EstimateMinutes, int LoggedMinutes, bool Done,
string? Tag, string? Project, DateOnly? Due, DateTime? RunningSince);

require.message: Keeps only the newest waiting snapshot

hints: `readonly Channel<T> pending = Channel.CreateBounded<T>(new BoundedChannelOptions(1) { FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.DropOldest });`
In the constructor: `worker = Task.Run(WriteAll);` where `async Task WriteAll() { await foreach (var s in pending.Reader.ReadAllAsync()) { await save(s); Saved++; } }`.
steps.explain: The channel is the only thing the two sides share, so there is no lock in sight. `DropOldest` with room for one is a *coalescing* queue: perfect when only the newest state matters. `sk` saves through your `Autosaver<Snapshot>` when a command changed something.
